newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: U.S. gives details of control of African force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives details of control of African force.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Thursday the United Nations would control and order peacekeeping missions carried out by a proposed African crisis force.

"The United Nations would have to take the decision to launch the mission and it would be under control of the United Nations as other peacekeeping endeavours, as other humanitarian endeavours," Christopher told representatives from the Organisation for Africa Unity (OAU).
But the mission would be "predominantly in the hands of those African countries that committed troops to the endeavour," he added, spelling out more detail on the still-evolving proposal.
OAU leaders raised concerns about who would control the force in their meeting with Christopher at OAU headquarters in Ethiopia.
Later, some diplomats, including OAU Secretary General Salim Ahmed Salim, said they were reassured by what he told them.
Salim also urged Washington to hold broader consultations and consider more African countries as potential participants, which U.S. officials said they would do.
Plans are to make the force operational in about six months.
Ethiopia is Christopher's second stop on a five-nation African tour. He also met Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi. He leaves Friday for Tanzania.
The 10,000-member all-African Crisis Response Force would be sent to countries where civil war, insurrection or campaigns of genocide threaten mass civilian casualties.
"It would not be a standing force but one that could be assembled quickly, led by Africans and deployed under U.N. auspices," Christopher said
The catalyst for the idea was Burundi's civil war, but the force could be used in other African countries, if needed.
Christopher suggested an even broader application, saying the force would protect innocent civilians, ensure humanitarian aid delivery and "help resolve conflicts in Africa and beyond."
He did not elaborate.
Various notions for a trained military force to act to prevent or respond to crises in Africa have been proposed and Christopher acknowledged it was not an original U.S. idea.
But with the United Nations and OAU unable to act quickly for lack of resources and other reasons, Washington seized the lead in organising and raising funds for such a force.
Christopher's strong embrace of the U.N. and OAU roles responded to Africans concerned Washington was acting unilaterally on what should be a multilateral endeavour.
The U.N. role could cause problems in the United States, which offered $30 million toward the force and where there is scepticism after U.N. disasters in Bosnia and Somalia.

Salim said the U.S. plan is consistent with Africa's new willingness to seek African solutions to African problems and to take responsibility for their continent without always looking to the international community for answers.
But he also said the OAU had concerns, including why Washington only approached 10 African states to join the force, who would command the force and how funding will be guaranteed.

Christopher said officials held initial talks with African countries who demonstrated interest, have experience in other peacekeeping missions, have civilian control over the military and "exhibit a sincere desire, not a mercenary desire."

As for funding, Christopher said Washington is discussing this with European and Asian allies because it too believes there must be "sustained support because none of us want to launch this kind of endeavour only to be frustrated by the lack of continuity and support."
